description: Sawing, shearing, laser cutting, lathe turning, milling, drilling and PCB etching explained.
content_html:
What Is Subtractive Manufacturing?

Subtractive manufacturing starts with a block, sheet or bar of material and removes unwanted sections until the finished part remains. Every process in this lesson — sawing, shearing, laser cutting, turning, milling and drilling — is subtractive. The removed material becomes waste (swarf, chips or offcuts), so material selection and planning the cutting sequence carefully both reduce cost and waste.

Cutting: Sawing, Shearing and Laser Cutting

The simplest subtractive operations separate a workpiece into pieces. Sawing uses a toothed blade — a hacksaw in the workshop or a band saw on the factory floor — to cut through metal, timber or plastics. The teeth are set (bent alternately left and right) so the kerf (slot) is slightly wider than the blade body, preventing binding.

Shearing uses two hardened blades (like giant scissors) to cut sheet metal without a kerf. A hydraulic guillotine can shear steel plate up to 10 mm thick cleanly and quickly. Because shearing requires no cutting fluid and produces no swarf, it is economical for straight-line cuts on sheet stock.

Laser cutting directs a high-power CO₂ or fibre laser beam onto the material surface. Controlled by CNC, it can cut intricate 2D profiles in metal, acrylic and timber with very narrow kerfs (as small as 0.1 mm) and no physical tool contact. Laser cutting is ideal for prototype sheet-metal brackets and signage panels but is limited to thin sections — typically below 25 mm for mild steel.

Key Fact

Sawing produces a kerf (slot) and swarf; shearing produces a clean cut with no kerf and no swarf; laser cutting produces a very narrow kerf and is CNC-controlled, allowing complex profiles to be cut automatically.

Turning on the Lathe

A lathe rotates the workpiece while a single-point cutting tool is fed along or into the material. Key parts of the lathe that examiners test regularly are:

  • Chuck — the rotating clamp at the headstock that grips the workpiece. A three-jaw self-centring chuck grips round or hexagonal bar automatically; a four-jaw independent chuck can grip irregular shapes.
  • Tailstock — the adjustable support at the opposite end of the bed. It can hold a live centre to support long workpieces, or a drill chuck for drilling on the lathe’s axis.
  • Carriage / tool post — holds the cutting tool and moves along the bed (for parallel turning) or across (for facing).
  • Bed — the precision-machined base that ensures the carriage moves parallel to the spindle axis.

Lathe operations include parallel (cylindrical) turning (reducing diameter along the length), facing (cutting across the end to produce a flat face), taper turning (angling the tool path to create a cone), and boring (enlarging an existing hole from the inside). Cutting speed and feed rate are set to suit the workpiece material — harder metals require slower speeds and a finer feed.

Every material has a recommended cutting speed (in metres per minute, m/min) — the speed at which the cutting tool moves through the material at the point of contact. For a rotating workpiece on a lathe, this depends on both the spindle speed (revolutions per minute, rpm) and the diameter of the workpiece.

The relationship is: $$N = \frac{1000 \times v}{\pi \times d}$$ where \(N\) = spindle speed (rpm), \(v\) = cutting speed (m/min), \(d\) = workpiece diameter (mm).

Worked example: A 40 mm diameter mild steel bar is to be turned. The recommended cutting speed for mild steel is 30 m/min. Find the required spindle speed. $$N = \frac{1000 \times 30}{\pi \times 40} = \frac{30\,000}{125.66} \approx 239 \text{ rpm}$$ The lathe would be set to the nearest available speed below 239 rpm to avoid over-speed and tool damage.

Notice that a larger diameter requires a lower spindle speed to maintain the same cutting speed at the surface. If the diameter halves, the spindle speed must double. This inverse relationship is a common exam question.

Milling

Milling uses a rotating multi-tooth cutter. Unlike a lathe (where the workpiece rotates), in milling the cutter rotates and the workpiece is clamped to a table that moves in X, Y and Z directions. Milling operations include:

  • Face milling — a large-diameter cutter with many teeth sweeps across the top surface to produce a flat, smooth face. Used to true-up castings and forgings.
  • Slot milling — an end mill (a cutter with teeth on its end and sides) cuts a slot or keyway into the workpiece surface.
  • Profile milling — the CNC table follows a programmed path to cut complex 2D or 3D shapes, used heavily in aerospace for aluminium wing ribs and in automotive for cylinder-head ports.
Key Fact

On a lathe the workpiece rotates and the tool is stationary (moves linearly). On a milling machine the cutter rotates and the workpiece is clamped to a moving table. Getting this the wrong way round is a common exam mistake.

Drilling

A pillar drill (also called a drill press) holds a drill bit in a rotating chuck and feeds it vertically into the workpiece. Tool names examiners expect you to know:

  • Centre drill — a short, rigid combined drill-and-countersink used first to create a precise starting point, preventing the twist drill from wandering.
  • Twist drill — the standard helical drill for producing through-holes and blind holes. Flutes carry swarf out of the hole.
  • Countersink — a conical cutter that bevels the top of a hole so a countersunk screw sits flush with the surface.
  • Counterbore — a stepped cutter that enlarges the top of a hole to receive a cap-head bolt so its head sits below the surface.

The sequence for drilling a precision hole is: mark out the centre with a centre punch → use a centre drill to start the hole accurately → drill the through-hole with a twist drill at the correct speed → de-burr the hole edges. Giving “drill” alone in an answer is not specific enough; always state the type of drill bit.

Chemical etching is used to produce printed circuit boards (PCBs). The process is subtractive but uses chemistry rather than mechanical cutting. A blank PCB consists of a fibreglass substrate coated in a thin copper layer. The desired circuit pattern is printed onto the copper using UV-sensitive etch-resist film, which is exposed and developed. The board is then immersed in ferric chloride (iron(III) chloride) solution, which dissolves the unprotected copper while leaving the resist-covered tracks intact. After etching, the resist is removed, revealing the finished copper tracks. Chemical etching bridges the Manufacturing and Systems units because PCBs are the foundation of electronic circuits.
exam_tip_html: Exam questions on drilling often ask you to name specific drill types — “drill” alone scores zero. Always write “centre drill”, “twist drill” or “countersink”. For lathe-parts questions, make sure you can name and locate the chuck, tailstock, carriage and bed — half of students cannot describe the chuck or tailstock in detail. For spindle-speed calculations, show every step of working: write out the formula, substitute values with units, then calculate. Method marks are awarded even when the final answer is wrong, so setting out the formula correctly is worth marks on its own.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Subtractive processes (sawing, shearing, laser cutting, turning, milling, drilling) all remove material from a workpiece — each suits different shapes, quantities and materials. Shearing has no kerf or swarf; laser cutting is CNC-controlled for complex 2D profiles.
  • On a lathe the workpiece rotates; on a milling machine the cutter rotates. Lathe operations include parallel turning, facing, taper turning and boring. The spindle speed formula is \(N = \frac{1000v}{\pi d}\).
  • For drilling: always name the specific bit (centre drill first, then twist drill). Chemical etching is the subtractive method for PCB production, using ferric chloride to dissolve unprotected copper.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the function of the tailstock on a centre lathe?
A) It holds the rotating cutter and moves along the bed
B) It grips the workpiece and rotates it at the spindle speed
C) It supports the far end of a long workpiece or holds a drill chuck for axial drilling
D) It controls the depth of cut taken by the cutting tool
practice_questions.marks: C) It supports the far end of a long workpiece or holds a drill chuck for axial drilling [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the drill bit used first when drilling a precision hole, and state why it is used first.
practice_questions.marks:
Centre drill [1 mark].
It creates an accurate starting point to prevent the twist drill from wandering off-centre [1 mark].
[2 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A CNC milling machine is used to produce a slot 120 mm long in an aluminium plate. The cutter has a diameter of 10 mm and rotates at 3 000 rpm. The feed rate is 200 mm/min.

Calculate the time taken to mill the full length of the slot. Give your answer in seconds.
practice_questions.marks:
Time = distance ÷ feed rate [1 mark for method]
Time = 120 mm ÷ 200 mm/min = 0.6 min [1 mark]
0.6 min × 60 = 36 seconds [1 mark for unit conversion]
[3 marks — 1 mark per step; award method mark even if arithmetic wrong]

practice_questions.text:
A mild steel shaft of diameter 50 mm is to be turned on a centre lathe. The recommended cutting speed for mild steel is 30 m/min.

(a) Use the formula below to calculate the required spindle speed. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

Spindle speed (rpm) = (1000 × cutting speed) ÷ (pi × diameter)

(b) The engineer chooses a lathe setting of 150 rpm. Explain whether this is a safe choice.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Calculation: Multi-Step with Unit Conversion
practice_questions.marks:
(a) N = (1000 × 30) ÷ (3.14159 × 50) [1 mark for substitution]
= 30 000 ÷ 157.08 [1 mark for correct calculation]
= 191 rpm (accept 190-192) [1 mark]

(b) 150 rpm is below the calculated value of 191 rpm [1 mark]. This means the cutting speed will be lower than recommended, which is safer for the tool (less heat, less tool wear) but will increase machining time. Any setting at or below 191 rpm is acceptable.
[4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a printed circuit board (PCB) is produced using chemical etching. Your answer should include the materials and chemicals involved and the stages of the process.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any four of:
- Start with a blank PCB: fibreglass substrate coated with a thin copper layer
- Apply UV-sensitive etch-resist film; print or expose the circuit pattern onto it using UV light
- Develop the resist so that only the circuit tracks are protected
- Immerse the board in ferric chloride solution, which dissolves the unprotected copper
- Remove the board and strip the resist, revealing the copper circuit tracks
- Drill component holes; inspect/clean the finished board
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Ridgeworth Precision Parts Ltd makes small-batch aluminium components for the motorsport industry. The production manager is considering whether to use laser cutting or milling for cutting aluminium bracket profiles from 3 mm sheet.

Compare laser cutting and milling as methods of producing these aluminium profiles. In your answer consider: accuracy, material waste, tooling requirements and suitability for low-volume production.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Compare Two Processes or Methods
practice_questions.marks:
Accuracy: Both can achieve high accuracy under CNC control. Laser cutting achieves a kerf as small as 0.1 mm with no mechanical force on the workpiece; milling can achieve tight dimensional tolerances but the cutter exerts cutting forces that may require a robust workholding fixture.

Material waste: Laser cutting has a very narrow kerf so material loss is minimal; milling removes material as chips (swarf) and the cutter path width must be accommodated in the nesting plan.

Tooling: Laser cutting has no physical cutting tool to change or wear; milling requires end mills that dull and must be replaced, adding consumable cost.

Low-volume suitability: Both can be programmed from a CAD file with minimal set-up time, making both suitable for small batches. Laser cutting has faster set-up (no tool change, no workholding beyond sheet clamping); milling requires a fixture and tool selection. For 3 mm aluminium sheet profiles, laser cutting is generally faster and lower-cost per part at low volumes.

[6 marks — award for developed comparative points. At least two aspects compared for full marks. No marks for describing each process in isolation without comparison.]

knowledge_checks.q: On a centre lathe, which part grips and rotates the workpiece?
Which cutting process uses two hardened blades to cut sheet metal without producing a kerf?
On a lathe, the _____ supports the far end of a long workpiece or holds a drill chuck for axial drilling.
Chemical etching for PCBs uses _____ solution to dissolve the unprotected copper tracks.
Match each drill bit type to its purpose:
right: Creates an accurate starting point to prevent wandering
Produces a through-hole or blind hole with helical flutes
Bevels the top of a hole so a countersunk screw sits flush

flashcard_questions.q: What does subtractive manufacturing remove material to produce?
flashcard_questions.a: A finished part from a larger block, sheet or bar of material.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the kerf in sawing?
flashcard_questions.a: The slot of material removed by the saw blade's teeth.

flashcard_questions.q: What rotates on a lathe — the workpiece or the cutter?
flashcard_questions.a: The workpiece rotates; the cutting tool moves linearly.

flashcard_questions.q: What rotates on a milling machine — the workpiece or the cutter?
flashcard_questions.a: The cutter rotates; the workpiece is clamped to a moving table.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the formula for spindle speed on a lathe.
flashcard_questions.a: N = (1000 × cutting speed) ÷ (pi × diameter), giving rpm.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a larger workpiece diameter require in terms of spindle speed?
flashcard_questions.a: A lower spindle speed to maintain the same surface cutting speed.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of a centre drill?
flashcard_questions.a: To create an accurate starting point and prevent the twist drill from wandering.
Sweeping a large-diameter cutter across a surface to produce a flat, smooth face.

flashcard_questions.q: What does laser cutting use to cut material?
flashcard_questions.a: A focused beam of coherent light (CO2 or fibre laser), controlled by CNC.

flashcard_questions.q: What chemical is used in PCB chemical etching to dissolve copper?
What is boring on a lathe?
flashcard_questions.a: Enlarging an existing hole from the inside using a boring bar.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must shearing be used only for straight-line cuts on sheet metal?
flashcard_questions.a: The two straight blades cannot follow a curved path — a shaped die or laser is needed for curves.

glossary_terms.definition: Any manufacturing process that removes material from a workpiece to achieve the desired shape, such as cutting, turning, milling or drilling.
A cutting process that uses a focused beam of coherent light to melt or vaporise material along a programmed path, cutting complex 2D profiles from sheet material.
A machine tool that rotates a workpiece on its axis while a stationary cutting tool is fed along or across the workpiece to remove material and produce cylindrical shapes.
A subtractive process in which a rotating multi-tooth cutter removes material from the surface of a workpiece that is fed past the cutter, producing flat faces, slots, pockets and complex profiles.
A chemical process that removes unwanted copper from a PCB blank by immersing it in ferric chloride solution, leaving the protected circuit tracks intact.
